title: When Asking for Help, Appeal to People's Self-Interest, Never to their Mercy or Gratitude
summary: Plead the other party's gain, never their memory of past favors. Charity is a debt people hurry to forget.
core: Help is rarely given out of affection or moral obligation. People confronted with an appeal to mercy or to past favors feel embarrassed, because they would have to acknowledge a dependence they never chose, and most quietly decline. The law advises reframing every request so that the person being asked can identify a concrete gain from granting it, and placing that gain at the centre of the appeal. The implied judgement is that generosity is a fiction people agree to maintain in conversation but not to fund in practice. Appeals grounded in it carry a silent accusation, and are read as evidence of weakness.
observance: The Medici bank of Florence built its influence on precisely this footing. From its Rome branch the family supplied the papal curia with credit and remittance services at a time when the Holy See was chronically short of cash, so that Florentine financiers were indispensable rather than merely welcome. The arrangement placed Lorenzo de' Medici's family at the centre of papal finance and helped deliver three popes. The papacy received what it wanted, reliable money. The Medici received access, standing, and a family position near the middle of European power. Nothing was begged, no loyalty was invoked, and no past favour was put forward as an argument, since the Medici had learned that appeals to gratitude only produce embarrassment and silence.
transgression: Louis XVI chose a different route in 1789. Facing a ruinous deficit, the king summoned the Estates-General after 175 years of silence and addressed the assembly as a peacemaker whose duty was to rescue the realm, expecting the nobles and clergy he had served to answer a call of personal loyalty. Instead the two privileged orders closed ranks to protect their tax exemptions, and deputies of the Third Estate declared themselves the National Assembly in June. Appeals built on duty and on the royal personality produced deadlock, mob politics, and within four years the monarchy itself was gone. The assumption that long service is repaid in kind proved fatal to the man who made it.
reversal: The law describes a transaction, not a moral endorsement. Leading every exchange with what benefits the other party turns relationships into permanent negotiation, and any hint of sincerity reads as manipulation once it is detected. Instrumental appeals also fail with people who cannot be bought and who judge a proposal on its own terms, on behalf of a cause or an idea that stands without them. In practice the strongest position keeps both elements: something worth backing for its own sake, and an honest account of what the patron gains.

title: Pose as a Friend, Work as a Spy
summary: Friendship is the cheapest cover for surveillance. The person who seems nearest to you may be reporting to your rival.
core: The law advises cultivating relationships primarily as a route to information about people whose intentions cannot otherwise be verified. Because open inquiry makes one an obvious enemy, the effective observer is disguised as a harmless friend, a guest, a servant, or a sympathetic listener. Trust creates access that interrogation could never buy, and the material gathered matters less for its facts than for what it reveals about character. The judgement is that goodwill is an instrument rather than a condition of power, and that anyone disclosing more than they appear to know is usually reporting upward.
observance: Louis XI of France constructed such a system between 1461 and 1483. Known at the time as the Universal Spider, he established a relay of postal posts across France so that his own correspondence moved faster than any rival court could intercept it, and he seeded the resulting network with informants drawn from merchants, clerics, servants, and lovers, people placed where news actually formed before it reached anyone official. Their reports let him anticipate conspiracies while they were still gossip and before they hardened into revolt, and he travelled almost constantly so that no great noble could predict when he would arrive or how many men would come with him. Information, not siege engines, dismantled the great feudal houses of France.
transgression: Edward IV of England trusted friendship and paid for it. William Hastings, Lord Chamberlain and the king's closest associate, was among the few men Edward believed without reservation; when the king died in April 1483 Hastings promptly wrote to Richard, Duke of Gloucester, reporting the death and urging him to come to London with a force to intercept the twelve-year-old Edward V. Hastings believed he was managing a dangerous succession in the royal interest. Richard had other intentions, arrested him on the road, and had him beheaded a fortnight later. A friend who reports elsewhere is an informant, and the intimacy that concealed the arrangement also stripped Hastings of any defence.
reversal: The law states a tactic, not a virtue. Espionage corrodes the relationships it exploits: people who suspect surveillance conceal everything, including what the ruler most needs to know, and a court known to run on informers eventually produces the counter-intelligence that destroys it. Domitian's execution of Epaphroditus, who had been Nero's own secretary and closest servant, around 95 AD shows the other hazard, since suspecting the people nearest to oneself manufactures paranoia from proximity alone. The sounder practice is to gather what can be learned openly and to reserve the covert channel for what genuinely cannot be obtained another way.

title: Crush your Enemy Totally
summary: An enemy left standing is a campaign postponed. Half-measures toward a defeated rival return as larger wars within a few years.
core: Enmity does not dissolve when a rival loses a battle. It survives in the person who lost and in the network that gathers around him. The law therefore treats the neutralization of a threat as indivisible, insisting that a commander who can still marshal men and money has finished nothing. The reasoning is arithmetic rather than sentimental, since a surviving enemy can rebuild, recover allies, and choose both the ground and the hour of the next contest. The judgement implied is that leniency has a long memory, and that generosity shown to someone capable of retaliation is indistinguishable from deferring the cost of the fight to another decade.
observance: The contest between the founder of the Han dynasty and the State of Chu is the textbook case. Xiang Yu, the stronger battlefield commander, defeated the future Emperor Gaozu repeatedly and repeatedly allowed him to escape, most starkly at the feast at Hongmen, where he let his rival slip away rather than kill him. Liu Bang used each reprieve, drew Xiang Yu's generals and troops to his own side over two years, and finally massed Han Xin and Peng Yue against Chu. At Gaixia in 202 BCE Han forces surrounded Xiang Yu while his men sang of a homeland already surrendered, and he retreated with fewer than eight hundred soldiers and died. The Han dynasty began.
transgression: Napoleon's abdication in 1814 was a negotiated mercy extended by the powers that had defeated him. He was permitted to rule Elba rather than face execution or imprisonment, and the restored Bourbons allowed him to keep the title of emperor. The generosity produced exactly what leniency invites. In February 1815 he escaped, marched on Paris, and resumed power while Louis XVIII fled to Ghent. Within a Hundred Days the Seventh Coalition mobilized again, Napoleon lost at Waterloo in June, and he was shipped to Saint Helena, where he died in 1821. The island chosen for its defensibility held him for six years, and the war it was meant to end cost Europe a great deal more than severity would have.
reversal: The arithmetic of the law fails in ways worth anticipating. Some defeated people are genuinely finished, and destroying them converts a settled quarrel into a martyrdom that recruits new enemies. Severity also licenses cruelty that outlives its purpose and hardens a ruler into the kind of coalition that money, marriage, or diplomacy would have split. And the assumption that every survivor will recover understates how many are harmless once removed from their position. The judgement is not that mercy is weakness, but that deliberation belongs before the verdict rather than after it.

title: Use Absence to Increase Respect and Honor
summary: Constant availability is its own punishment. What is rare is read as valuable; what is always there is taken for granted.
core: Value in the eyes of others rises as availability falls. Someone seen every day becomes furniture, a fact of the environment, and is judged by the ordinary rather than the exceptional. The law advises withdrawing, shortening appearances, and letting absence supply what flattery cannot: a question that others must answer themselves, in imagination, and answer generously. Presence, by contrast, imposes the observer's judgement directly. The implied judgement is that most people do not evaluate what they are shown every day; they evaluate the interval, the scarcity, and the freedom from obligation they associate with a person they rarely see.
observance: Louis XIV turned the French crown into the most guarded thing in Europe by refusing to be ordinary. At Versailles the king followed a timetable so minutely observed that access became currency: nobles who could claim even a small part of the levee or coucher outperformed men of far greater birth, and courtiers understood that the reward for service was a moment of his presence. The ritual itself enforced distance, since the great audience rooms could be entered but not crossed, and the man at the centre was visible and unattainable at the same time. Seniority in the new hierarchy was measured in proximity, which is the most stable of all measures because it cannot be faked.
transgression: Louis XVI abandoned the machinery his predecessors had built. He disliked the ceremonies, took refuge in his private apartments, and let the public routines grow rarer until, as the later Versailles records note, courtiers complained they never saw the king at all. With the rituals went the distance that the rituals produced, and the royal household became an ordinary domestic one with an ordinary master. Louis's son took his lessons in a tower, and the monarchy was reduced to an anxious private household surrounded by a city that had quietly stopped finding its king impressive. He spent the crisis years in a prison, wrote his defence in the form of a school exercise, and was guillotined in 1793 having never once in his reign appeared as a rare thing.
reversal: The tactic depends on prior standing; used carelessly it reads as neglect. A leader who vanishes when subordinates need him teaches them that reliability is optional, and the imagination the absence invites usually fills the space with something worse than the truth. The practical correction is to ration rather than to withhold, and to reappear predictably enough that the return itself carries weight. Scarcity also backfires on the person hiding: Elizabeth I remained both unmarried and secluded, and the same fears of vulnerability that produced her mystique fed endless speculation at her expense for the last two decades of her life.

title: Keep Others in Suspended Terror: Cultivate an Air of Unpredictability
summary: Never let an opponent know what you will do next. Terror holds its force only while the next move remains unreadable.
core: The law argues that power is exercised through the imagination others build about one's intentions. A person whose reactions are always the same can be managed, because the reaction can be calculated and provoked at will. One who remains unreadable forces every subordinate and rival to behave as though any moment might bring a reversal, and in that state of suspension people become cautious, deferential, and careful with their own designs. The judgement is that predictability is the flaw that power cannot repair after it has been observed, and that the terror itself, once it stops being intermittent, stops working.
observance: Aurelian, emperor of Rome from 270 to 275, cultivated a reputation that contemporaries could not settle. His soldiers knew him as an iron fist, and the Historia Augusta records him moving between sudden violent resolutions against revolting senators and conspicuous mercy toward surrendered cities and conquered rulers. He personally broke off a campaign against the city of Tyana after its appeal rather than besieging it, and left the city untouched. The refusal to be predictable was itself exploited by his own officers, who forged a document naming them as condemned men and killed him on the strength of it in 275, precisely because his fear of conspiracy had become an expectation.
transgression: Abraham Lincoln was killed because he was predictable in the one way that mattered to his enemies. He had survived a rifle shot on the road to his summer cottage in 1864 and reasoned afterward that an incompetent hunter was the likeliest explanation, then kept the matter quiet. He continued to accept public appearances without protection, and when John Wilkes Booth had earlier considered kidnapping him, the president's habit of going to the theatre whenever his duties allowed had made the timing obvious. On the evening of 14 April 1865 Lincoln sat in Ford's Theatre. The openness that made him approachable is what made him reachable, and he died the next morning.
reversal: Unpredictability and terror are not the same instrument. Terror applied evenly breeds the conspiracies it was meant to prevent, and the ruler whose capriciousness becomes well understood is more dangerous to himself than to anyone else; Aurelian died because his own officers finally worked out what the pattern meant. The tactic also corrodes the judgment it is meant to sharpen, since people who expect to be destroyed stop offering real counsel and offer only what they think will spare them. The more durable form is procedural rather than temperamental: consistent rules applied without favour, which produce caution without producing panic.

title: Do Not Build Fortresses to Protect Yourself - Isolation is Dangerous
summary: A fortress protects the walls and cuts off the supply of everything else: news, allies, and the warning that comes before danger.
core: The law treats the fortified retreat, the guarded house, the closed household as a false solution. A wall keeps out the enemy but also keeps out the people who report on the enemy, and a leader who cannot see clearly cannot correct course before events close around him. Isolation converts a visible threat into an invisible one, which is exactly the condition under which power dissolves without anyone laying a finger on it. The judgement is that protection which removes the ruler from the flow of events is not protection but a slower form of defeat, and that the only real security is being difficult to isolate in the first place.
observance: Louis XI of France governed from the saddle. He travelled across his kingdom throughout his reign rather than holding court in one fortified place, and the postal relays he established gave him a communication network that let information travel outward from every region to him faster than it could reach any rival. Because he was never stationary and never predictable in his movements, the great feudatories of the Loire could not plan against him, and they could not approach him without their approach becoming known. The architecture he was defeating, in other words, was other people's fortresses, and the habit of presence dissolved them faster than any siege could have done.
transgression: Louis XVI's family spent their last two years in the tower of the Temple, and the conditions of their confinement were themselves the punishment. Communication with the outside was cut, the guards were hostile, and the family's contact with the political life of France stopped almost entirely. On 20 November 1792 a strongbox was found in which the king's letters to foreign powers, proposing a counter-revolution, had been concealed; it was opened by a committee and became the immediate justification for his trial. He had built his fortress, lost the stream of information, and inside it he was surprised by everything he had not known, including the depth of the hatred and the ease with which former friends supplied evidence.
reversal: The law does not argue for carelessness; it argues against the specific error of treating distance as a protective asset. A defence that depends on remaining unreachable is only as good as its last forecast, and once contact is lost the last forecast is a guess. Nor can isolation be maintained without diverting the attention that should be going outward: the hidden ruler spends it on being hidden. The workable version is a person who is difficult to reach, never difficult to attack, and who accepts that the surest protection is being the figure others most need to come to.

title: Know Who You're Dealing with - Do Not Offend the Wrong Person
summary: An insult is safe against the powerless and fatal against the patient. Discernment is the whole discipline.
core: The law treats hostility as a deployment decision rather than a mood. Not every enemy deserves the same effort and not every one can be absorbed if provoked: some are courteous and forget, some are petty and dangerous, and some are weak now and formidable later. The prudent actor identifies which kind is in front of them, spends outrage only where it produces advantage, and above all avoids the gratuitous slight that converts a neutral party into a permanent adversary. The judgement is that most wars are started by men who mistook a slight for an opportunity, and that the ability to hold back is rarer and more useful than the ability to strike.
observance: Louis XI read the Church correctly and did not provoke it. France in the 1470s was full of grievances against papal interference, and kings who thundered about them paid for it in lost authority; Louis instead negotiated the concordat of 1472, through which he secured the right to control episcopal appointments in France while leaving Rome's dignity and the appearance of papal precedence untouched. He took the substance and left the grievance unexpressed, which is the whole difference between winning the argument and losing the war over it. The arrangement gave the French crown control of its own clergy for a generation of bishops trained and appointed at home, and it did so without creating a papal enemy or the domestic factionalism that blunt attacks on Rome had handed to his predecessors.
transgression: Henry III of France murdered the one man he could not afford to attack in open politics. Henry I, Duke of Guise, led the Catholic League, was backed by Spain and the papacy, and had the London example of Mary, Queen of Scots before him; the king responded by having the duke killed in Paris in 1588, in circumstances that left Henry himself unable to claim responsibility. The League survived its leader and turned on the king, and on 2 August 1589 Jacques Clément, a Dominican friar from the League's own network, stabbed Henry at Saint-Cloud. The men who insulted Henry out of all proportion to his position were the ones who finally destroyed him.
reversal: Caution applied indiscriminately produces its own failure, because a ruler who cannot be provoked at all cannot be provoked into acting either. Louis XVI had this problem in its purest form: he refused to crush faction after faction, pardoned the leaders of each, and twice refused the death penalty for treason, reasoning that a king who killed his own subjects could not then expect their loyalty. By 1792 no one in France feared the office. Refusal to offend is sound as a discipline against needless enemies and useless as a substitute for the willingness to punish the ones who have earned it.

title: Do Not Commit to Anyone
summary: Allegiance given without reserve is a hostage handed over. Power survives the loss of its patron, and dependence does not.
core: The law advises never to place one's fortunes entirely in another person's hands, however strong the attachment and however visible the favour. A committed ally becomes the property of the person they serve: their talent, their access, and their enemies all belong to the patron, and when the patron falls the entire structure falls with them. The disciplined alternative is to be useful to several centres at once and to owe each of them only what they are presently owed. The judgement is that political weather changes faster than most people imagine, and that the person who owns nothing outside one relationship owns nothing at all once the relationship reverses.
observance: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand outlived every regime he served, which is the entire point of the example. He served Louis XVI, then the Revolution, then Napoleon as foreign minister, resigned in 1807, and continued to advise Napoleon while openly working with Tsar Alexander I and Metternich toward his master's defeat. When the Bourbons returned in 1814 he was again useful, becoming president of the provisional government that welcomed the Allied armies and then foreign minister at Vienna, where he negotiated France's return as a great power. Under Louis XVIII he was first grand chamberlain and prime minister, lost that post to the ultras, and survived again, returning to office in 1830. He died in 1838, at eighty-four, having outlived four changes of government.
transgression: Thomas Wolsey built himself into the extension of a single man and called it service. He was Henry VIII's chief minister for fourteen years, called the alter rex, and shaped the king's decisions so completely that the historian John Guy found Henry taking independent decisions only in the broadest sense. When Henry wanted an annulment that Clement VII would not grant, Wolsey made it the whole purpose of his foreign policy and put his own office on the line for it. In 1529 the pope had the case sent to two legates, Campeggio stalled until the proceedings lapsed, and Wolsey was stripped of his offices within months. He was then charged with treason, the standard instrument for a minister the king no longer wished to protect.
reversal: Non-commitment has a cost that is usually paid later. A person who owes everyone a little is trusted fully by no one, and the moment a single patron is genuinely necessary, the wide network offers no one to call. Talleyrand survived by being indispensable to a sequence of masters rather than by being especially liked by any of them, and that is a colder form of security than loyalty, not a better one. The workable version distinguishes what can be held from what can be committed: never the whole reputation, the whole income, or the whole future in one relationship, but never the withholding of visible loyalty either, since suspected disloyalty ends more careers than switching does.

title: Play a Sucker to Catch a Sucker - Seem Dumber than your Mark
summary: The person who is read as harmless is the one nobody prepares for. Understatement is the cheapest armour available.
core: The law treats apparent capability as an invitation. A person who reveals how sharp they are invites the best counter they face, whereas one who appears ordinary, easy, faintly harmless, or simply uninterested is not studied and is not defended against. The advice is to undersell deliberately in negotiation and in rivalry, letting the other side believe they have measured the whole of the strength available to them. The judgement is that most people arrange their defences around the version of you they have seen, and almost none of them will look for the second set of hands beneath the obvious ones.
observance: Louis Philippe, Duke of Orléans, spent twenty-one years in exile after 1793 and had been judged and found harmless by every faction in France: republicans, émigrés, and the Bourbons each assumed the cadet Orleans branch would never amount to anything. When he took the throne in 1830 he cultivated the image rather than correcting it, presenting himself as the Citizen King, a plain citizen in trousers rather than a crowned figure, and the pose held for eighteen years. It absorbed two assassination attempts, the first by Giuseppe Fieschi in 1832 and a second by Jean-Jules-Antoine Lepeletier de Saint-Fargeau in 1840, both of which assumed a man so mild that approach required only a long knife. He was not overthrown by the establishment but outlasted most of the men who had counted him out.
transgression: Commodus turned the same instinct into a performance that destroyed him. Rome's emperor entered the arena as a gladiator, fought in public against armed men while dressed in the costume of a fighter rather than a ruler, and then asked the Senate to watch the display in person so that they might observe how much they depended on him. The senators would not attend. Having spent his reign making himself the man in the room who was least like a king, he could no longer ask the room for anything, and in December 192 a wrestler he had publicly humiliated in the arena took his life. Playing the fool is a discipline about what others believe you can do; demonstrating that you have stopped caring whether they respect you is not the same act.
reversal: The tactic presupposes a private competence that the public performance conceals, and when that competence is thin the disguise only removes the last warning. Emperor Claudius had genuinely been written off as a natural idiot, his own mother used him as a byword for stupidity, and being harmless is what kept him alive through the purges of Tiberius and Caligula. But Suetonius records that the inconsistency of his rulings as judge, now shrewd, now careless, now merely silly, so discredited him that he was held in general and open contempt. Nobody fears a man who has been seen clearly and found wanting, and the underestimation that protected Claudius for a decade turned into the disregard that left him defenceless.

title: Use the Surrender Tactic: Transform Weakness into Power
summary: An unconditional concession buys the one thing force cannot: the moment when the other side lowers its guard and commits.
core: The law proposes that a position with no margin can sometimes be converted into advantage by giving something away so completely that the giver appears finished, and by then taking what an opponent who believes the game is over will not be guarding. It is the logic of feigned collapse, used by those who know that the moment of triumph is when a rival's defences are at their thinnest. The judgement is that strength spent against a surrendering opponent buys only the opponent, and that what matters is what the aggressor then does not expect. The method depends on timing and on having something left to play, which is what separates the tactic from capitulation.
observance: After the Battle of Ankara in 1402 Timur had destroyed the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I and taken him prisoner, and had every political reason to erase the man and with him the memory of the Ottomans being great. He did the opposite. Bayazid was confined but kept alive, honoured as a captive king rather than executed as a criminal, and the Anatolian beyliks that had risen against Bayezid were left to their own rulers rather than being folded into the empire. A living sultan was worth more to Timur than a dead one: he was a title, an occasion for ransom and marriage negotiations, and a living demonstration that the Ottomans were finished. The captivity that should have ended the dynasty instead became the instrument by which Timur held Turkey in place for the rest of his life.
transgression: Charles I of England surrendered the wrong way and at the wrong moment. Defeated at Naseby in June 1645 he withdrew into the walled cathedral at Southwell and gave himself up to the Scottish army, hoping that a Stuart in Scottish hands and the Scots' fear of a second Charles Stuart at their own gates would bind them to him. The Scots were in fact outmanoeuvred by Parliament, who used their custody to break the parliamentary army's pay and clothing, and in January 1649 they handed him over to Westminster. A king whose surrender has bought nothing has surrendered everything: he gave up the last physical fact that made men hesitate, and the refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the court that tried him ended only in the execution at Whitehall.
reversal: The surrender tactic fails in exactly the case where it is most tempting, because the moment of total collapse is also the moment the opponent stops listening. A gesture of concession will be accepted at face value only if the recipient expects it, and once the offer has been made there is no way to withdraw it without conceding that the gesture was theatrical; the captor is then free to treat the surrendered party as worthless, which is exactly how Timur's captive Bayezid was used for the rest of his life and how Charles I was treated by everyone who handled him after 1645. The manoeuvre is only available to a person already counted as nothing and owed nothing.

title: Concentrate Your Forces
summary: Superiority in one place defeats an enemy who is superior everywhere else. Weight decides; numbers only decide once assembled.
core: The law states the arithmetic of advantage: force committed in one direction is worth several times the same force spread thin, and a general who subdivides his army into equal parts has guaranteed that every part will be beaten in detail. Concentration also concentrates information, since a single command sees a single field. The judgement is that possession of a greater total of men, money, or influence is not possession of power until it is gathered at a single point, and that the dispersion which looks prudent, spreading risk across many positions, is the surest way to lose everywhere at once.
observance: Frederick II entered the Seven Years' War in 1756 with a third of Austria's forces against her, France, Russia, and Sweden, and in November 1757 he turned that disadvantage into the battle that decided the opening phase of the war. At Rossbach the Franco-Imperial army had assembled in a crescent far larger than the Prussian force, so dispersed and so linked to its many separate commissariat and command connections that Frederick was able to move against a single seam, strike there with everything he had, and roll up a force that outnumbered him heavily. The Prussian victory destroyed the impression of invincibility that had carried the alliance, and Frederick then held the coalition at bay for the rest of the war with a much smaller army.
transgression: Napoleon's campaign of 1812 dispersed his army across an empire rather than concentrating it against anything. The invasion force moved as a column, but detachments peeled off continuously to garrison and to feed the line: Oudinot was defeated and pinned at Smolensk, Napoleon's own corps was turned back from the Vitebsk approach, Macdonald was held at the Berezina by Wittgenstein and nearly destroyed, and Kutuzov avoided a decisive engagement until Moscow was lost. Each separate body met a concentrated force in front of it, and when the Army of the Centre came west through the snow the operation was over. The empire had more soldiers than the Russians; not one point had more soldiers than the Russians.
reversal: Concentration carries its own bill. A single committed force has no second chance, and an opponent who identifies where it is gathered needs only one well-aimed stroke; the campaign of 1812 killed tens of thousands of men in exactly that way, first at the crossing points, then in the retreat. The correction is concentration with a reserve kept out of the plan: the mass in one place, a smaller body held back, and never a single line of advance that one defeat can sever.

title: Play the Perfect Courtier
summary: Influence at court is not won on merit. It is won by the endless, careful performance of being useful and never difficult.
core: The law describes the courtier as a role rather than a rank: a person of evident ability whose entire outward behaviour is directed at making the prince the source of every good idea and the only credible centre of decision. The obligations are endless and unglamorous, because every advance has to be manufactured rather than announced and every slight absorbed without a visible wound. The judgement is that at court the substance of what one says matters less than the perfection with which one decorates it, and that the man who competes on substance alone has already declared a contest whose rules he has not read.
observance: Benvenuto Cellini's own account of his dealings with Francis I is the clearest surviving record of the art being practised by someone who knew it was an art. At Fontainebleau he made himself necessary in a way that cannot be separated from his flattery, currying favour with the king and the royal mistress while the siege was being raised around the town, and he later recorded with satisfaction that Francis had asked for his help specifically. His position was never secure and he knew it. He was at once treasured as a maker of wonders and suspected of theft; the courtiers at court disliked him, and twice escaped the capital to avoid arrest. He died in his own house in Paris in 1571, having outlived the king by decades while others who had managed the court better were forgotten sooner.
transgression: Anne Boleyn came to power by being conspicuous in a court that rewards inconspicuousness. She made her appeal visible, in dress, in proximity to the king, and in the open rivalry with the princess whom she served, and she made an enemy of Thomas Cromwell when he was a nobody she was free to dismiss and later a minister whose help she could not spare. Her position depended entirely on the king's favour with no second pillar anywhere in the kingdom, and when that favour lapsed in 1536 there was no one to speak for her: she was accused, tried by a court staffed by her declared enemies, and executed in May. What a courtier loses is not a battle but the position, and having never been anything but a favourite, she had no second position to fall back on.
reversal: The performance has a terminal condition. Baldesar Castiglione described the perfect courtier at length, in a book that became the handbook of the European court for a century, and died poor in 1529; the ideal he documented had no place in the world that produced him. The slower cost is the credit: a person who has spent a life arranging that others take it finds nothing recorded under his own name. The workable version keeps one competence strictly private and measures advancement by access to the decision rather than by applause in the room.
